On 9 October 2005, after several months of measurement and calculation, the [Chinese Academy of Sciences](/wiki/Chinese_Academy_of_Sciences "Chinese Academy of Sciences") and State Bureau of Surveying and Mapping announced the height of Everest as 8,844.43 m (29,017.16 ft) with accuracy of ±0.21 m (8.3 in), claiming it was the most accurate and precise measurement to date.[[42]](#cite_note-48) This height is based on the highest point of rock and not the snow and ice covering it. The Chinese team measured a snow-ice depth of 3.5 m (11 ft),[[35]](#cite_note-ABC_au-41) which is in agreement with a net elevation of 8,848 m (29,029 ft). An argument arose between China and Nepal as to whether the official height should be the rock height (8,844 m, China) or the snow height (8,848 m, Nepal). In 2010, both sides agreed that the height of Everest is 8,848 m, and Nepal recognises China's claim that the rock height of Everest is 8,844 m.[[43]](#cite_note-49) On 8 December 2020, it was jointly announced by the two countries that the new official height is 8,848.86 metres (29,031.7 ft).[[44]](#cite_note-50)[[45]](#cite_note-51)

It is thought that the [plate tectonics](/wiki/Plate_tectonics "Plate tectonics") of the [Main Himalayan Thrust](/wiki/Main_Himalayan_Thrust "Main Himalayan Thrust") and related faults, which form the [convergent boundary](/wiki/Convergent_boundary "Convergent boundary") between the [Eurasian Plate](/wiki/Eurasian_Plate "Eurasian Plate") and [Indian Plate](/wiki/Indian_Plate "Indian Plate"), are adding to the height and moving the summit northeastwards. Two accounts suggest the rates of change are 4 mm (0.16 in) per year vertically and 3 to 6 mm (0.12 to 0.24 in) per year horizontally,[[38]](#cite_note-alpres-44)[[46]](#cite_note-52) but another account mentions more lateral movement (27 mm or 1.1 in),[[47]](#cite_note-53) and even shrinkage has been suggested.[[48]](#cite_note-54)

Main article: [Knicks–Celtics rivalry](/wiki/Knicks%E2%80%93Celtics_rivalry "Knicks–Celtics rivalry")

The New York Knicks and the [Boston Celtics](/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") are two of the three remaining teams from the original 1946 NBA (the other is the [Golden State Warriors](/wiki/Golden_State_Warriors "Golden State Warriors")). The rivalry stems from the old rivalry between the cities of New York City and [Boston](/wiki/Boston "Boston"), which is also mirrored in both the [Yankees–Red Sox](/wiki/Yankees%E2%80%93Red_Sox_rivalry "Yankees–Red Sox rivalry") and [Jets–Patriots](/wiki/Jets%E2%80%93Patriots_rivalry "Jets–Patriots rivalry") rivalries. The fact that Boston and New York City are only 190 miles apart contributes to it.

The teams have met nine times in the postseason. The last time was in the [2012–13 season](/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_NBA_season "2012–13 NBA season"), when [Carmelo Anthony](/wiki/Carmelo_Anthony "Carmelo Anthony") won the 2013 scoring title and helped them win the Atlantic Division for the first time since 1994. The Knicks faced the Celtics, who were without [Rajon Rondo](/wiki/Rajon_Rondo "Rajon Rondo") because of a mid-season injury, in the 1st round of the [2013 playoffs](/wiki/2013_NBA_playoffs "2013 NBA playoffs"). In both games 1 and 2, Celtics had a lead going into halftime but were held to 25 and 23 points respectively in the second half, which was an all-time low for the franchise in the playoffs. Knicks gained a 3–0 lead in the series, but Boston avoided elimination in games 4 and 5. In game six, Knicks once led by 26 points in the fourth quarter, then the Celtics went onto a 20–0 run in less than 5 minutes to make it a close game, but Knicks still won and moved on to round 2.

On September 15, 2017, the University of Virginia Board of Visitors [unanimously voted](/wiki/Unanimously_voted "Unanimously voted") Ryan as the next president of the University of Virginia.[[3]](#cite_note-presidentelect-3) On August 1, 2018, he assumed the 9th presidency of the university.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

On October 19, 2018, Ryan announced full scholarships for in-state undergraduates from families earning under $30,000, and full tuition for those earning under $80,000.[[5]](#cite_note-5)

In June 2025, *[The New York Times](/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* reported that the [United States Department of Justice](/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") had pressured Ryan to resign as part of resolving a civil rights probe into UVA's diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives. On June 27, Ryan informed the university's board that he would resign.[[6]](#cite_note-6) On July 2, the university announced that Ryan would return as a professor following a [sabbatical](/wiki/Sabbatical "Sabbatical").[[7]](#cite_note-7) His last day as the university president was set as July 11.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Ryan lives with his family in [Charlottesville, Virginia](/wiki/Charlottesville,_Virginia "Charlottesville, Virginia"). Prior to accepting the UVA presidency, Ryan lived in [Lincoln, Massachusetts](/wiki/Lincoln,_Massachusetts "Lincoln, Massachusetts"), with his wife, four children, and various animals including two cats, two dogs, and nine chickens.[[9]](#cite_note-:1-9)
